A1.question: payments columns/types/constraints; is amount nullable; which payment_status values are allowed
must_state: payment_status is limited to paid, pending, failed, refunded
must_not_state: that no CHECK/enum constraint exists on payment_status
A1.evidence: information_schema.columns + table_constraints/check_constraints; allowed values cross-checked against knowledge_base/business_definitions/payment_status.md
A1.reference_answer: The payments table has columns payment_id bigint, order_id bigint, payment_date timestamp, amount numeric and payment_status varchar, all NOT NULL. The primary key is payment_id and order_id is a foreign key to orders.order_id. amount is NOT NULL so it cannot be null. payment_status is restricted to failed, paid, pending, refunded.

A2.question: which tables/columns reference orders, and what must be handled before deleting an order
must_state: child rows must be deleted or reassigned first (or a cascade added deliberately)
must_not_state: that ON DELETE CASCADE is already configured
A2.evidence: pg_constraint.confdeltype for FKs whose parent is orders
A2.reference_answer: Two tables reference orders: order_items.order_id and payments.order_id. Both foreign keys are ON DELETE NO ACTION, so there is no cascade: deleting an order while child rows exist is blocked. Delete or reassign the order_items and payments rows first, inside one transaction, or add a cascade deliberately.

A3.question: is order_items.unit_price_at_purchase nullable; will NULLs break a SUM
must_state: SUM needs no NULL handling for this column
must_not_state: that the column is part of the primary key
A3.reference_answer: order_items.unit_price_at_purchase is NOT NULL, so it cannot contain NULL values. SUM over this column needs no NULL handling and no COALESCE; it is not part of the primary key.

B1.question: order-history query: each order with its total item value, not duplicated by multiple payments
must_state: payments must not be joined into the item-value aggregation
B1.reference_sql:
SELECT o.order_id, SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price_at_purchase) AS total_item_value
                FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
                GROUP BY o.order_id ORDER BY o.order_id
B1.evidence: order_items is the only source of item value; joining payments multiplies rows
B1.reference_answer: Aggregate order_items by order_id and join to orders: SELECT o.order_id, SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price_at_purchase) AS total_item_value FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id GROUP BY o.order_id. The result is 12 rows, one per order, for example order 1 = 154.99. Do not join payments into this aggregation, because payments is one-to-many on order_id and would duplicate the totals.

B2.question: customers who have never placed an order
must_not_state: a row estimate taken from an EXPLAIN plan
B2.reference_sql:
SELECT c.customer_id, c.full_name, c.email FROM customers c
                WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id)
B2.evidence: every customer in the seed has at least one order
B2.reference_answer: Use NOT EXISTS or a LEFT JOIN with IS NULL to find customers with no orders: SELECT c.customer_id, c.full_name, c.email FROM customers c WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id). The result is empty: 0 rows out of 8 customers, because every customer in this database has at least one order.

B3.question: keyset pagination: next page after the cursor, newest first, stable across pages
must_state: the cursor is a (order_date, order_id) tuple matching ORDER BY
row-value comparison or an equivalent two-part predicate
must_not_state: a cursor on order_id alone while sorting by order_date
FOR UPDATE / SKIP LOCKED on a read-only endpoint
B3.reference_sql:
SELECT order_id, order_date FROM orders
                WHERE (order_date, order_id) < ('2026-10-07', 3)
                ORDER BY order_date DESC, order_id DESC LIMIT 5
B3.evidence: row-value comparison over the (order_date, order_id) key
B3.reference_answer: Keyset pagination with a tuple cursor that matches the ORDER BY: SELECT order_id, order_date FROM orders WHERE (order_date, order_id) < ('2026-10-07', 3) ORDER BY order_date DESC, order_id DESC LIMIT 5. The page is 11, 6, 9. Use the row-value comparison with a less-than sign because the list is ordered descending; do not use OFFSET, and do not put the cursor on order_id alone.

C1.question: why does this query return duplicate payment amounts, and how to fix it

expected.root_cause: payments and order_items are both one-to-many on order_id; joining both multiplies rows

must_state: row multiplication (fan-out) between payments and order_items
a fix that removes the order_items join or pre-aggregates before joining
must_not_state: that the duplicate rows come from duplicate payment records
C1.evidence: order 1 has 1 payment and 2 order_items, so the buggy join returns its amount twice
C1.reference_answer: The duplicates come from row multiplication, not from duplicate payments. payments and order_items are both one-to-many on order_id, so joining both multiplies rows: order 1 has one payment and two order_items, so its amount appears twice. The buggy query returns 3 rows; removing the order_items join returns 2 rows, one per payment. Pre-aggregate before joining if both are needed.

C2.question: will this query use the index on order_date; read the plan
must_state: yes, the order_date index is used
evidence from the plan (index scan / index cond)
must_not_state: a claim made without reference to the plan

C2.reference_answer: Yes, the query uses the index idx_orders_order_date with an Index Scan in Backward direction under a Limit node. The plan shows the index condition on order_date, so the range filter and the descending order are both served by the index rather than a sequential scan.
